messages.subject_clean: Query regarding GSoc'15 project "Convex optimization modeling language" in R
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I am Ayush Pandey, junior undergraduate at IIT Kharagpur pursuing Mathematics & Computing Sciences.

While browsing through R projects for GSoc'15, I found Convex optimization modeling language <https://github.com/rstats-gsoc/gsoc2015/wiki/Convex-optimization-modeling-language> project interesting and something very exciting to work on. I have recently taken course on Operation Research in which i have mainly studied Linear Programming(Github <https://github.com/Ayush-iitkgp/Linear-Programming>). I think this project is the extension of what i have studied and pretty much will to work on it.

But sadly there is no mentor assigned for this project, will the mentor be assigned to me by the organisation ? Please guide me what can be done in this regard so that i can work towards a successful GSoc project.

Yours Sincerely,
Ayush Pandey
LinkedIn Profile <https://www.linkedin.com/pub/ayush-pandey/66/9/a52>
GitHub <https://github.com/Ayush-iitkgp>

messages.body_plain:
Dear Brent,

The key difference between shiny and RIGHT lies in whether the client or the server supports the basic interactivity, such as hovering and brushing among linked plots. Shiny, together with ggvis, supports most of the interactivity, including the basic ones, from the server side. (Shiny alone can only provide static plots.) For instance, if a graphical element is selected, the updates are made through the server-side code. RIGHT tries to support basic interactivity from the client side, your browser. This makes certain operations more responsive at the cost of implementing plotting routines in JavaScript. For more complex interactivity, RIGHT relies on shiny and server-side R code.

RIGHT still has a long way to go to become as mature as shiny or ggvis. Unfortunately, the key developers of the RIGHT package lack time to support a GSoC project this year, and we feel sorry about that.

Sincerely,
Junghoon Lee

Students must submit project applications on melange.

The student application process is open till the end of next week.
Incomplete applications will be disallowed by the R GSoC Administrators.

As in past years, all R student applications will be rated by all R
mentors.

While the applications are being commented on and rated by the R
mentors, the R GSoC Administrators will request slots from Google based
on the number of mentors and high quality applications for projects
received.

prior years.

As has been the case in prior years, once Google grants us slots, we
will award them to the top rated projects and applications.

both mentors who have never participated in GSoC, mentors who we cannot
verify, and in most but not all cases projects where both mentors are
from the same institution (especially if you have no prior GSoC
experience).

It is also important that per Google program guidelines (you clicked on
them in melange), communication with students during the application
period be limited to feedback on their applications.  Only Google can

This has been a long-standing guideline of R's participation in GSoC.

Some of this information was on the old sciviews R wiki, which was
unfortunately taken down rather suddenly.

All of the things I mentioned are guidelines built from many years of
R's participation in GSoC.  All of them have been broken at one point or
another, and usually hinge on comfort with the student proposals and
mentor preparation. (To this last point, is is promising that you
mention that you have been preparing for a long time for your mlr projects.)

Another guideline which you are running up against is that you propose
three projects for your first GSoC.  As Michel should be able to tell
you, GSoC is a *lot* of work for the mentors as well as the students.  I
personally will be very unlikely to support not one but *three* projects
from a group of participants among whom only one has any GSoC experience.

First, you would have to have three really excellent proposals, such
that they filtered to the upper grouping of the voting.

Next, you, as mentors, would have to make clear how you are going to
make time to mentor that many students.  It has been done. I was primary
mentor on one project, and listed as co-mentor on three others a few
years ago.  Of those, I had significant involvement in two of the
projects I was co-mentoring. In this my experience is much like the
model you're proposing.

That summer, I spent 30+ hours per week mentoring those GSoC projects.
I have not tried to do that in subsequent years, because it is just too
much of a commitment in addition to my full time work at the office.  Do
you and your co-mentors *each* have that much time?

Finally, R would have to receive enough slots from Google for all of
your projects to get slots.  I'm sure you can understand that slots are
a finite commodity, and giving three slots to one group and zero slots
to other projects if applications are comparable would not be fair.

So, is this a hard and fast rule? No, not at all. Will it be an issue
for you?  That depends first on the quality of your applications.  Only
if you get excellent student proposals for all three of your proposed
projects and R asks for and receives lots of slots will we be having a
conversation about whether you and your co-mentors really have the time
to dedicate to this.

Brian

messages.body_plain:
Now that the student application process is open, I thought I would take
a moment to provide some information for both students and mentors.

As in prior years, we have project standards if you want your project to
get a slot.

Students:

Proposed project idea pages are here:

https://github.com/rstats-gsoc/gsoc2015/wiki/table-of-proposed-coding-projects

Details on the project, and mentor contact details for questions, should
be there.

The application template is here:

https://github.com/rstats-gsoc/gsoc2015/blob/master/RWiki/student_app_template.txt

All applications will be reviewed and ranked by all R mentors.

Applications that do not contain at least the minimum information in the
template *will not* get a slot.

The best applications run to several pages if printed, and show
considerable thought and planning.  The application process is longer
this year than it has been in some prior years, so this should not be a
problem.

Once your draft application has been submitted, you may receive comments
from other R mentors, either listed project mentor or others.  Please
respond to the comments promptly and completely.  Being non-responsive
before you've even been awarded a slot is not a good sign for the
success of your proposal.

Google's deadlines are firm, we don't control them, and can't allow late
submissions.

Mentors:

If you have not already done so, you need to sign in or register on
melange, fill out your profile and accept the terms, and initiate a
connection request to the 'R Project for Statistical Computing'. Please
make the org admin's lives easier and identify yourself and your project
idea page in your connection request.

Please make sure that your email (and ideally your melange link id) are
on your project idea page, we do ask the students to provide this
information in their applications.

If you and all your co-mentor(s) have the same university or company
affiliation, you need to find a mentor from some other institution.  We
try to spread things around a bit, and gather different perspectives.
If two of you are from the same institution, please find a third
co-mentor from somewhere else.

If you are a first time GSoC mentor, I sincerely hope that you have an
experienced co-mentor.  GSoC is a lot of work, and we try to avoid
mentors disappearing or being overwhelmed in the middle of the summer.

If you don't have a co-mentor, you need to find one!  Projects will not
be approved with only one mentor, *especially* if you have no GSoC
experience (see above).

All mentors are encouraged to review all proposals that they feel
competent to comment on any aspect of.  Please help all our potential
students and mentors create better projects by asking questions and
making suggestions.  As in prior years, there are 'public' comments that
the student will see, and 'private' comments that only the other R
mentors will see for our internal discussion.

Please do not hesitate to email this list, me, or any of the other R
GSoC organization administrators with any questions.

Regards,

Brian

--

I know you guys are also putting a lot of work into this, as a
suggestion these things could be mentioned
in the wiki upfront the next time. I have no problem asking people but
in this case I simply didnt know about the constraints and simply
followed what was on the current wiki.

I will put up further background info page on us mentors now, so you
know who you are dealing with.

> Another guideline which you are running up against is that you propose
> three projects for your first GSoC.  As Michel should be able to tell
> you, GSoC is a *lot* of work for the mentors as well as the students.
> I personally will be very unlikely to support not one but *three*
> projects from a group of participants among whom only one has any GSoC
> experience.
>
> First, you would have to have three really excellent proposals, such
> that they filtered to the upper grouping of the voting.
>
> Next, you, as mentors, would have to make clear how you are going to
> make time to mentor that many students.  It has been done. I was
> primary mentor on one project, and listed as co-mentor on three others
> a few years ago.  Of those, I had significant involvement in two of
> the projects I was co-mentoring. In this my experience is much like
> the model you're proposing.
>
> That summer, I spent 30+ hours per week mentoring those GSoC projects.

> office.  Do you and your co-mentors *each* have that much time?

>

> for you?  That depends first on the quality of your applications.
> Only if you get excellent student proposals for all three of your
> proposed projects and R asks for and receives lots of slots will we be
> having a conversation about whether you and your co-mentors really

I am mainly mentoring the hyperparameter / tuning project, that I am

The visualization project is mentored by 2 other very competent people.
As our software is like  I said not small, I am mainly "guiding" here,

For the ensemble one, Aydin is the main mentor nad has also done lots of

something work.

Best

Bernd

they are qualified to do so.

This includes private comments, not seen by the student, designed to be
seen and discussed by the other mentors.  When we vote, mentors are
asked to comment specifically on reasons for *downvoting* a particular
application to aid the R GSoC administrators in making close calls

questions focused on the project at hand.  For example, if the schedule

disclosed conflicts with full-time GSoC participation.  Public comments
should be aimed primarily at helping the student improve their
application.  Think of it like a grant application (it is one), and the
time between now and the close of the application period is for the
committee of mentors to ask questions and make suggestions aimed at
helping the student improve that application.

You are certainly encouraged to comment both publicly and privately on
applications for your projects.  Public comments, as described above.
Private comments are typically limited to describing things like your
confidence in the application, or disclosing any prior contacts that
would make you comfortable spending the summer working with that student
(or conversely, reservations that you have about it), or to discussing
private comments from other mentors.

Brian

We ask all R mentors to comment on and rate all proposals that they feel
qualified to do so on, using private comments to comment on the things
that should be only discussed among the mentors, and public comments for
things students should respond to, as I described in my note on public
and private comments yesterday, and my longer note from last week.

3 Apr is not a Google deadline.  It an R org deadline. By the middle of
the scoring period, we need to have some idea of which student proposals
will likely drop out.  One way that we can assess that is whether the
mentors are engaged, which means in melange and participating in the
ranking and commentary.  In some prior years, we had only a few days
from the close of the application period to the slot request.  Last
year, iirc, we had a week.  This year, we have two weeks between the
application deadline and the slot request deadline, so given that it is
clear that not all mentors listed on the ideas wiki are in melange right
now, we need to give people notice that they need to get into melange.
